title: Three config levels, and why your commits have the wrong email
summary: System, global and local config stack on top of each other. Learn which one wins, how to see where a value came from, and how to stop committing work email to personal repos.
mental_model: Git reads system, then global, then local, and the last one to speak wins. Every confusing config problem is answered by `git config --list --show-origin`, which prints the value *and* the file it came from.

steps.title: See what identity you would commit with
steps.why: There is no local setting yet, so git falls back to the global one — your work identity. Every commit you make in this personal repo would carry it, forever, in a field that cannot be edited without rewriting history.
steps.expect: The email resolves to the global file.

steps.title: Commit once and look at the damage
steps.why: Author and committer email are baked into the commit object. This is why the fix has to happen before you commit, or via a history rewrite afterwards.

steps.title: Set a local identity — local beats global
steps.why: `--local` writes to `.git/config` inside this repo only. It is the narrowest scope and therefore the winner. Nothing about the global file changes.

steps.title: Prove where each value comes from
steps.why: `--show-origin` prints the file behind every value. When a setting behaves in a way you cannot explain, this one command ends the argument in seconds.
steps.expect: user.email listed twice — once global, once local. The local one is the effective value.

steps.title: Fix the commit that already went out
steps.why: `commit --amend --reset-author` rewrites the last commit with the currently configured identity. It only works for commits you have not shared; for older ones you would need a history rewrite.

verify.label: the commit now carries the personal email

steps.title: Settings worth turning on everywhere
steps.why: These three prevent whole categories of confusion: pull.rebase stops merge-commit litter, rerere remembers conflict resolutions, and push.default=simple refuses to push branches you did not mean to.

verify.label: this repo commits with the personal identity
the global identity was left alone — local overrides, it does not replace
the existing commit was corrected too

pitfalls: Setting `user.email` after committing does not fix past commits. The identity is part of the commit object.
`git config --global core.excludesfile` is the right home for editor and OS noise like .DS_Store — do not put it in every project's .gitignore.
Conditional includes (`[includeIf "gitdir:~/work/"]`) switch identity by directory automatically. It is the real fix for the work/personal split.
This sandbox has its own throwaway global config — nothing you do here can reach your real ~/.gitconfig.
cheatsheet: the effective value after all three levels
every value and the file it came from
remove a value at that level
redo the last commit with the current identity
